result:
Solutions 1 and 2 are wrong because they claim F_{N-1} is non-standard, but it is standard. Solution 1 only considers constant central multipliers μ_X = c·id, and Solution 2 assumes every standard pair has ξ = 1. Both miss degree-dependent transformations.

Take μ_X^i = u^{-i}·id on each X^i, where u = 1+x^{N-1}. On minimal complexes the differentials have entries in (x), so x^{N-1}d = 0 and μ is a chain map. Scalars that depend only on degree commute with every degree-0 chain map, so μ is natural on the minimal skeleton, which determines the whole category. The shift condition μ_X[1]∘ξ_X = μ_{X[1]} holds, since μ_X[1] has degree-i entry u^{-(i+1)} and multiplying by ξ = u gives u^{-i}. So (id, ξ_{N-1}) is triangle naturally isomorphic to (id, id), which is standard via T = A_N. This rules out b_N = N-1.

Solution 3 correctly identifies F_{N-1} as standard. Its claim that F_{N-2} is a non-standard triangle autoequivalence is plausible but not fully verified here. The triangle property is monotone in e, so it suffices that F_{N-2} is a triangle autoequivalence. Its explicit obstruction, based on the trace criterion, gives a threshold of about ⌊2N/3⌋, which is at most N-2 for N ≥ 6. Its non-standardness argument for e ≤ N-2 is also plausible. The N ≥ 7 hypothesis is not explained by this argument, so I have some residual uncertainty about the exact answer.

CHOICE: 3
